plan.chapterName: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, chapter 10: Liquids and Solids
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a single energy-level schematic relating the enthalpy changes of the phase transitions among three states of matter. A black vertical arrow along the left edge, labeled Energy, points upward and sets the vertical scale; no numerical values appear anywhere. Three horizontal blue lines cross the diagram at increasing heights, labeled at their right-hand ends Solid at the bottom, Liquid about a third of the way up, and Gas near the top, with the solid-to-liquid separation noticeably smaller than the liquid-to-gas separation. Three thick red arrows point upward between these levels. The leftmost spans the full distance from the Solid line to the Gas line and is labeled Sublimation, delta H sub. Just to its right a shorter arrow rises only from the Solid line to the Liquid line, labeled Fusion, delta H fus, and directly above that arrow a third one continues from the Liquid line to the Gas line, labeled Vaporization, delta H vap. Placing the one long arrow beside two stacked shorter arrows that together cover the same vertical distance lets the additive relation among the three quantities be read straight off the drawing. The layout supports modeling sublimation as melting followed by vaporization so that the enthalpies of the individual steps can be summed.

interactionPlan.concept: The enthalpy change for sublimation equals the sum of the enthalpy changes for fusion and vaporization because enthalpy depends only on the initial and final states.

interactions.teaches: The same Solid-to-Gas energy difference can be represented either as one direct sublimation step or as two stacked steps through the liquid state

demo_steps.title: Direct Solid-to-Gas transition
demo_steps.narration: In the direct view, the single red sublimation arrow spans the full energy gap from the Solid level to the Gas level. That full vertical distance represents ΔH_sub.

demo_steps.title: Switch to the two-step path
demo_steps.narration: The same start and end levels can be reached by first melting the solid and then vaporizing the liquid. The long sublimation arrow is replaced by two stacked arrows.

demo_steps.title: Add fusion
demo_steps.narration: Step to Liquid: the fusion arrow lights up and the running total grows from the Solid level to the Liquid level. This first contribution is ΔH_fus.

demo_steps.title: Add vaporization
demo_steps.narration: Step to Gas: the vaporization arrow lights up above the fusion arrow, and the running total reaches the Gas level. Together, ΔH_fus and ΔH_vap span the same height as ΔH_sub.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Because enthalpy is a state function, ΔH_sub = ΔH_fus + ΔH_vap for the same Solid-to-Gas change.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Use a clean 2D energy-level schematic with no numerical scale. Place the black Energy axis vertically on the left and three blue horizontal levels across the figure: Solid lowest, Liquid above it, Gas highest. Make the Solid-to-Liquid gap visibly smaller than the Liquid-to-Gas gap. In direct view, emphasize the single long red sublimation arrow from Solid to Gas. In two-step view, emphasize the stacked red fusion and vaporization arrows in the same vertical span. Use bright highlighting only for the current active arrow in the phasePath sequence, and show a simple vertical running-total marker growing upward from Solid to Liquid to Gas.

authoredContext:
Consider the extent to which intermolecular attractions must be overcome to achieve a given phase transition. Converting a solid into a liquid requires that these attractions be only partially overcome; transition to the gaseous state requires that they be completely overcome. As a result, the enthalpy of fusion for a substance is less than its enthalpy of vaporization. This same logic can be used to derive an approximate relation between the enthalpies of all phase changes for a given substance. Though not an entirely accurate description, sublimation may be conveniently modeled as a sequential two-step process of melting followed by vaporization in order to apply Hess’s Law. Viewed in this manner, the enthalpy of sublimation for a substance may be estimated as the sum of its enthalpies of fusion and vaporization, as illustrated in the figure. For example:

For a given substance, the sum of its enthalpy of fusion and enthalpy of vaporization is approximately equal to its enthalpy of sublimation.

A diagram is shown with a vertical line drawn on the left side and labeled “Energy” and three horizontal lines drawn near the bottom, lower third and top of the diagram. These three lines are labeled, from bottom to top, “Solid,” “Liquid” and “Gas.” Near the middle of the diagram, a vertical, upward-facing arrow is drawn from the solid line to the gas line and labeled “Sublimation, delta sign, H, subscript sub.” To the right of this arrow is a second vertical, upward-facing arrow that is drawn from the solid line to the liquid line and labeled “Fusion, delta sign, H, subscript fus.” Above the second arrow is a third arrow drawn from the liquid line to the gas line and labeled, “Vaporization, delta sign, H, subscript vap.”

discrepancies: In the default state, the fusion and vaporization arrows and their labels are faded to low opacity, whereas the source shows all three red arrows and all labels equally prominent.

The generated figure adds a yellow glow around the sublimation arrow, a green running-total marker, and a boxed equation annotation that are not present in the source and visually clutter the textbook-style diagram.
The enthalpy labels use awkward/incorrect subscript rendering such as ΔHₛᵤᵦ and ΔHfᵤₛ/ΔHvₐₚ rather than the clear source labels ΔH_sub, ΔH_fus, and ΔH_vap.
The source shows a plain red sublimation arrow, but the generated default highlights it with an extra yellow outline and makes it visually dominate the figure.
The vaporization and fusion labels are gray/faded in the default screenshot, reducing legibility and making them look secondary despite being core labels in the source.
evaluation.notes: The basic energy-level layout and arrow topology are recognizable, but the default state is not a faithful static replacement because key arrows are faded and several interactive explanatory overlays are visible.
action_items: Make the default view match the source: show sublimation, fusion, and vaporization arrows and labels at full opacity with no active highlighting.
Remove or hide the yellow glow, green running-total marker, and equation box unless the user activates an explanatory interaction.
Format the enthalpy labels to clearly read ΔH_sub, ΔH_fus, and ΔH_vap, with consistent black text matching the source.
Keep the red arrows plain and equal in stroke weight/color in the default static state.
